conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. I see you came in with abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same pain I always get. Right in the middle, kind of dull but it’s been worse the last two days. I’ve been nauseous too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you been able to eat or drink much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I feel full fast. And I haven’t taken my insulin the past two days… I just didn’t feel like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. Your blood sugar was very high when you arrived—490. And we found ketones in your urine, which means you were in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: DKA? I’ve had that before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can be. It happens when your body doesn’t have enough insulin and starts breaking down fat for energy, which creates acids. But we’ve started treatment—IV fluids and insulin—and your levels are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so tired. And anxious. I just want this pain to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re tearful and anxious, which we’ve seen before. We’ll keep managing your pain and anxiety. We’ve continued your sertraline and lorazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve had so many admissions for this pain. No one ever finds a cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s tough. Your history shows chronic abdominal pain, possibly related to diabetic gastroparesis and stress. We don’t see signs of infection or blockage now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have fever or burning when I pee. Just the nausea and fullness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your urine shows white blood cells and bacteria, but no symptoms of UTI, so we’re not starting antibiotics. It may be from your urethral diverticulum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also placed a central line in your neck to make giving fluids and insulin easier. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot, no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt that. It was uncomfortable, but I knew it was needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your blood sugar is down to 220 and your anion gap has closed. That means the DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I have something to drink? I’m thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start clear liquids. But slowly—your stomach may still be slow to empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look much better. Glucose is 140, sodium is stable, and your kidney function is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. Still nauseous, but the pain is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch you back to your regular insulin—54 units glargine at bedtime and 10 units humalog with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I missed doses. I get overwhelmed. My mom’s cancer came back… it’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry to hear that. Your mental health matters. We’ll keep your sertraline and amitriptyline. And your PCP will set up a visit with a diabetes nurse practitioner in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. I need more support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re inserting a port-a-cath later today to help with future blood draws and IV access, since you’ve had infections from lines before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had that blood infection before. A port would be better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port was placed successfully. You’ll heal in a few days. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel safer knowing I won’t need so many needle sticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is still high—16,000—but it’s been high for years. Hematology isn’t concerned. Likely due to chronic inflammation and diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. No fever, no new symptoms. We’re not treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat real food tomorrow? I’m so tired of broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try soft foods tomorrow if you keep tolerating liquids. But small portions—gastroparesis means your stomach empties slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. Your labs are stable: glucose 69, sodium 132, creatinine 1.3. Your DKA is resolved, and you’re hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. Continue all your medications, especially insulin. A nurse will call to set up your follow-up in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try not to miss doses. I know it’s dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. And your daughter will be involved in your care, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s picking me up. I’m glad to have her support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and call if your sugar goes too high or low, or if pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.
